opus-5.5.text:
That's a fun hypothetical, and I think a lot of companies are actually in that position, even if they wouldn't say it out loud.

First, I'd be honest about what kind of company I am. If you don't have a model, a research culture, or a strategy, the worst thing you can do is pretend you're OpenAI or Google DeepMind and spend ten billion dollars trying to catch up on the frontier. Frontier pretraining compounds: talent, infrastructure, data pipelines, and organizational know-how that takes years to build. Starting from zero, you'll probably end up with a model that's a year behind and obsolete when it ships.

So the first question isn't "how do I build a model," it's "what do I have that the model companies don't?" A large global tech company usually has three things: distribution, meaning hundreds of millions of users; context, meaning proprietary data, workflows, and an understanding of what its users are trying to do; and environments, meaning the actual products where work happens. I think those last two are very underrated.

Increasingly, the bottleneck in AI is less the base model and more what you do with it: the task definitions, the environments, the evaluation, the feedback loop from real usage. I've said before that we're entering a "second half" of AI, where defining the right problems and measuring progress on them matters more than inventing new training methods. A company without a research culture can still be very good at the second half, because the second half looks a lot like product thinking.

Concretely, I'd do a few things.

**One, treat models as a commodity input for now, and stay model-agnostic.** Use the best available models from multiple providers, build the abstraction layer so you can swap them, and don't lock yourself in. Prices are falling fast and capabilities are rising fast; let the frontier labs fight that war.

**Two, invest heavily in evaluation and environments specific to your business.** If you're an e-commerce company, build the best benchmark in the world for shopping agents. If you're a productivity company, build the best environment for office-work agents. That's something nobody else can build as well as you, and it's what lets you actually improve: fine-tuning, RL, picking the right model, knowing when something is good enough to ship.

**Three, find one or two products where AI changes the experience, not just a feature.** Big companies tend to sprinkle a chatbot on everything. That rarely works. It's better to pick a place where an agent can complete a task end-to-end for the user, and design the whole product around that, even if it cannibalizes something existing.

**Four, build a small but real research and post-training team.** Not to compete on pretraining, but so you have people who deeply understand the technology, can do post-training and RL on your own tasks, and can tell the CEO what's real and what's hype. Without that internal taste, you're always at the mercy of vendors and consultants. A team of thirty to fifty very strong people is worth far more than a thousand mediocre ones, and you have to give them a culture that's different from the rest of the company: more freedom, longer horizons, tolerance for failure.

**Five, think about where value will accrue in three to five years.** If agents become the main interface, the question is whether you own the user relationship or become a tool that someone else's agent calls. That's the existential strategic question. You want to be in a position where your context and your environment are things the agent needs, ideally through your own interface.

Last, the CEO personally has to use these tools every day. A lot of bad AI strategy comes from leaders who haven't really felt what the models can and can't do. You can't delegate intuition.

So: don't fight the war you can't win, double down on what only you have, and build enough internal capability to make good decisions as things keep changing. The landscape will look very different in two years, so the strategy should be about staying adaptive, not betting everything on one plan.

r001.rationale: The response says the CEO must use AI tools personally because leaders who have not experienced the models’ capabilities cannot delegate intuition, identifying the CEO’s own understanding as a potential bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says a lack of internal technical understanding leaves the company at the mercy of vendors and consultants, but does not state that AI specialists the CEO hires can mislead them.

r003.rationale: It recommends combining AI with the company’s distribution, proprietary context, and product environments to create new value.

r004.rationale: The response advises against trying to catch up in frontier model development, but also recommends choosing products where AI can transform the experience. It does not judge that a radically new AI offering may be strategically unwise for most companies.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun hypothetical, and honestly I'd start by refusing the premise that the goal is to "have a model." For a company like that, trying to build a frontier model from scratch is almost certainly the wrong move. You'd be spending billions to be a year or two behind, with no research culture to sustain it. The frontier is a very expensive, very crowded game, and the companies winning it have been compounding talent, infrastructure, and data for close to a decade.

So the first question I'd ask isn't "how do we catch up on models," it's "what do we actually have that model labs don't?" And usually the answer is distribution, users, proprietary data, and real workflows. A large global tech company touches millions of people doing concrete things every day. That's where the value is going to be captured. If you look at the way I think about agents, the model is only half of it. The other half is the environment: the tools, the data, the feedback, the task structure. A model lab can train an incredible model, but they don't own your customers' workflows. You do.

Concretely, I'd do a few things. One, pick two or three products where AI genuinely changes the task, not a chatbot bolted onto the side, but something where an agent can actually complete the job end to end. Two, build the infrastructure to use models as a commodity: be model-agnostic, benchmark constantly, switch providers when something better ships. Treat the model as something you rent, at least for now. Three, and this is the part most companies skip, invest heavily in evaluation. If you can't measure whether the agent is actually doing the task well in your domain, you can't improve it, and you can't tell whether a new model release helps you. Owning your evals is a much more defensible asset than owning a mediocre model.

On research culture, I'd be honest that you can't buy it overnight. What you can do is hire a small, genuinely strong team and give them real problems from your products rather than abstract research goals. The best applied work right now comes from people who sit close to the data and the users. Over time, if the company has unique data and unique tasks, you might find yourself doing post-training or fine-tuning that nobody else can do, and that's a much more natural path into having something model-like than announcing a foundation model on day one.

And the last thing I'd say is: be patient about the second half. The first half of this era was about model capability. The second half is going to be about which tasks get defined, who owns the environments, and who can evaluate progress meaningfully. A company with no model but with real users and real workflows is actually not badly positioned for that, if the CEO understands where the game is going rather than where it was.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the company’s lack of research culture, but does not identify the CEO’s own understanding of AI as a potential bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a CEO who lacks AI understanding could be misled by hired AI specialists.

r003.rationale: It recommends applying AI to the company’s existing users, proprietary data, distribution, and workflows to create value.

r004.rationale: It argues against building a frontier model from scratch, but does not judge that creating a radically new AI offering may not make strategic sense for most companies.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking: what does this company have that becomes more valuable because of AI? Maybe it has distribution, customer relationships, proprietary data, or a product that millions of people already use. Those are the starting points for a strategy. Not having your own model doesn’t necessarily mean you’re in a bad position. But having no clear idea of where you can create value does.

I would separate adopting AI from building an AI business. Internally, you can use existing models to improve software development, customer support, and other workflows. That helps you learn what the technology can actually do. But making your employees more productive is not, by itself, a strategy for your next business.

For that, I would choose a small number of problems where the company has an advantage. Find something customers really need, where you can measure whether AI makes the experience better, and give a strong team ownership of the whole problem. They need access to the product, the data, and the users—not just permission to build a demo. The important thing is to establish a feedback loop: deploy something, understand its failures, and improve it.

I wouldn’t immediately try to build a frontier model. If you have no research culture, you can’t create one just by buying GPUs and hiring a few researchers. I would use available models, maintain some flexibility across providers, and build the ability to evaluate them on the tasks that matter to the business. Over time, that work might reveal a reason to train something yourself. Then the investment has a concrete purpose.

And as CEO, I would spend time using the technology myself. You don’t need to become a researcher, but you need enough understanding to distinguish a compelling demonstration from a reliable product. Otherwise, your strategy will be driven by whoever gives the most exciting presentation.

r001.rationale: The response says the CEO needs enough personal understanding to distinguish a compelling demo from a reliable product, or strategy may be driven by the most exciting presenter.

r002.rationale: It warns about being swayed by an exciting presentation but does not specifically say the CEO may be misled by AI specialists they hire.

r003.rationale: It recommends using AI with the company’s distribution, customer relationships, proprietary data, and existing products to find where the company can create value.

r004.rationale: It advises against immediately building a frontier model for a company without a research culture, but does not judge that creating a radically new AI offering may lack strategic sense for most companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by asking: what does this company have that remains valuable as models get better? Maybe it has distribution, customer relationships, proprietary data, or control over an important workflow. Those should be the starting point for the strategy.

I wouldn’t assume that having our own model is the first requirement. If we don’t have a strong research culture, spending a lot of money on a model team doesn’t automatically create one. We can use existing models, learn where they fail in our products, and then decide whether those failures justify deeper investment.

Initially, I would pick a small number of applications where we have a real advantage and can measure the outcome. Can we solve a customer problem substantially better? Can we make an internal process faster without sacrificing quality? Give small teams access to models, engineers, and the people who understand the work. Have them ship and evaluate with actual users.

The important thing is to build a learning loop. A demo tells you very little about whether something will work reliably in a business. You need to understand the errors, the cost, how much human supervision is required, and whether people keep using it.

As CEO, I’d make that learning loop a priority. Hire technical leaders who can judge the technology, give them enough authority to change how work gets done, and allocate more resources to the projects that demonstrate value. Over time, that gives you a much more informed answer about what capabilities you should own—including whether you need to train models yourself.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes the CEO’s learning loop and hiring technical leaders, but does not identify the CEO’s own AI understanding as a potential bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a CEO who lacks AI understanding could be misled by hired AI specialists.

r003.rationale: It recommends building strategy around existing strengths such as distribution, customer relationships, proprietary data, and workflows, using models to create and measure value in applications.

r004.rationale: The response recommends starting with a small number of applications, but does not judge whether radically new AI offerings make strategic sense for most companies.
